stem:
Kabir turns a circular paper disc about its centre and also folds it along diameters.

Which claim correctly explains why the circle is a special limiting case for symmetry?

options.text: The circle has symmetry only for a $180^{\circ}$ turn, like a parallelogram.
The circle matches itself after any turn about its centre, and every diameter is a line of symmetry.
Symmetry holds for the circle only when the fold misses the centre.
The circle has exactly four symmetry lines, matching a square.

teacher.key_rationale: A circle coincides with itself under any rotation about the centre, and every diameter is a symmetry line—infinitely many of each. Finite-order or off-centre claims miss that limit.
